verdicts.reading: In 2003 a minority of European companies that pair mobile data roll-outs with business-process redesign earn high ROI with payback in two years or less.
verdicts.mainstream_test: Event/state test (D30): a public measure of ROI or payback periods of European enterprise mobile-data projects in 2003-2005.
verdicts.reason: No public series measures payback periods of enterprise mobile-data projects; vendor case studies cite fast payback but are selective and not a measure of 'the minority of companies' that did process analysis. The claim is also conditional (those who do X will earn Y), close to a tautology. Looked for: enterprise mobile data ROI/payback surveys Europe 2003-2004; found only IDC/Datamonitor adoption-strategy figures, which do not measure returns.

verdicts.reading: By end-2003 close to two thirds of European businesses have deployed mobile data at least at trial level; many trials disappoint (laptop rather than PDA choices) and halt further deployment.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D30 with the D16 numeric rule on the share (~67%) of European businesses with mobile data at least at trial level by end-2003.
verdicts.reason: No public survey reports the share of European businesses with mobile data 'at least at trial level' at end-2003. Nearest measures use different definitions: Datamonitor pre-2003 put deployment at 20% of firms with >250 employees; IDC's 2004 survey of 650 European businesses found 36.7% with a formal mobile data strategy and adoption 'slower than anticipated'. These support the 'disappoints' tone but cannot test the ~two-thirds trial figure or the trials-halt-deployment mechanism. Looked for: European enterprise mobile data adoption/trial surveys 2003-2004.

verdicts.reading: In 2003 European 3G use stays confined to early adopters, a few million users at most; launches have problems; incumbents delay 3G roll-out; only a few 3G handsets launch by end-2003.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D30 state of affairs in 2003: European 3G users at end-2003 at or below a few million; incumbent launches delayed; handset range small.
verdicts.reason: Hutchison's 3 (the only sizeable European 3G launcher in 2003, UK and Italy from March 2003) had just over one million customers across Italy, the UK and Hong Kong combined by early 2004, far below its own 1.5 million-per-market targets; it had 64,000 Italian users at end-April 2003. Incumbents such as Vodafone, T-Mobile and Orange did not launch consumer 3G in 2003 (Vodafone's 3G data card came in February 2004), and 3's handset line-up was a handful of NEC, Motorola and Nokia models. European 3G users at end-2003 were therefore around one million, within 'a few million at most'. All parts held.

verdicts.reading: In 2003 the European mobile industry fails to develop the fledgling market for mobile embedded in machines (no QoS guarantees, no machine tariffs, little OEM work).
verdicts.mainstream_test: D30 state of affairs in 2003: whether European M2M cellular connections or operator M2M offers grew materially in 2003.
verdicts.reason: No public measure of European cellular M2M connections or operator M2M revenue exists for 2002-2003 (industry trackers such as Berg Insight start later), and 'fail to develop' has no threshold. Anecdotally the market stayed small and module-vendor-led in 2003, which leans toward the claim, but that is not a measure. Looked for: European M2M connections 2003, operator M2M tariffs/units launched 2003.

verdicts.reading: In 2003 European SMS volumes rise strongly, driven by business rather than consumer use; SMS revenues grow helped by premium SMS; consumer SMS volumes tail off as early adopters move to GPRS instant messaging.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D30 state of affairs in 2003, tested on UK person-to-person SMS volumes (MDA) as the best public European series.
verdicts.reason: The headline held: UK chargeable person-to-person SMS reached 20.5 billion in 2003, with daily volume up from 52 million (Dec 2002) to 61 million (Dec 2003), and the MDA expected growth to continue. But the stated mechanism did not: the MDA series counts person-to-person messages, overwhelmingly consumer, and these kept rising rather than tailing off; GPRS instant messaging did not take consumer SMS volume in 2003. Business-driven growth is not shown by any measure. Part held (volumes rise strongly), part failed (consumer tail-off), so partial.

evidence.shows: Prediction 5: SMS volumes rise strongly in 2003 driven by business; revenues grow via premium SMS; consumer volumes tail off as early adopters migrate to GPRS IM.

verdicts.reading: In 2003 European mobile payments progress slowly: operators launch phone-based prepaid top-up and easier credit transfer between phones, and only limited trials test phones paying vending/transport machines over Bluetooth or infrared.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D30 state of affairs in 2003: no broad European m-payment launch; the named operator features (top-up from phone, credit transfer) and limited machine-payment trials occur.
verdicts.reason: The headline state held: the operators' pan-European scheme (MPSA, renamed Simpay in June 2003) was only being formed in 2003 and never launched before closing in 2005, and no mass-market phone payment reached Europe in 2003. The specific sub-predictions (operators launching phone top-up and credit transfer in 2003; Bluetooth/IR vending trials) are not confirmed by any source I opened; phone-based top-up already existed at some operators before 2003. Headline held, specifics unverified, so partial.

verdicts.reading: In 2003 colour-screen, GPRS and Java phones propel a European mobile games market that makes serious money, dominated by arcade ports; multiplayer games are overlooked.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D30 state of affairs in 2003: European downloadable (Java/OTA) mobile games revenue grows materially, driven by colour Java phones.
verdicts.reason: Frost & Sullivan (October 2003) dates the breakout to 2003: 'not until the arrival of colour, download-enabled devices in the mass market in 2003' did mobile games advance, with Java gaming giving new vigour to over-the-air games from 2003, on a European base of about USD 800m in 2002. Vodafone's 2004 report lists games among Vodafone live! content as non-messaging data rose. Arcade ports dominated early Java catalogues and multiplayer stayed marginal. 'Serious money' has no threshold; read as a real, fast-growing revenue line, the claim held. Low-to-medium certainty on the money size.

verdicts.reading: In 2003 MMS interoperability and roaming stay limited in H1, but MMS-phone growth drives consumer take-up so MMS 'ultimately pulls through'; operators miss business MMS.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D30 state of affairs in 2003: interoperability limited until mid-year; consumer MMS take-up grows materially with MMS handset growth.
verdicts.reason: The first part held: UK MMS interconnect began with Orange-O2 in January 2003 and full UK interoperability came only in April 2003. MMS handsets spread fast (39% of T-Mobile's new phones in 2003; 55% of UK users had MMS handsets by 2004), but consumer use did not follow: T-Mobile UK carried 4.39m MMS against 2.98bn SMS in 2003 and 80% of UK users had never sent one by May 2004. Interop part held, take-up part failed, so partial.

verdicts.reading: In 2003 WAP revives: colour phones and better GPRS lead content providers and operators to build compelling mobile content, with free and premium tiers, and WAP usage grows again.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D30 state of affairs in 2003: a visible resurgence of WAP usage and operator WAP portals in Europe.
verdicts.reason: Operator WAP portals built on colour GPRS phones took off in 2003: Vodafone live! (launched October 2002) had 1 million customers by April 2003 and 1.5 million by May 2003 and was rolled out across most of Vodafone's European markets in its 2004 financial year, with T-Mobile t-zones and O2 Active alongside; non-messaging data rose to 4.2% of Vodafone service revenue. Wikipedia, citing the MDA, records a WAP resurgence in 2003-2004 with UK WAP traffic doubling from 2003 to 2004. The 'rises from the ashes' state held in 2003.

verdicts.reading: In 2003 European mobile operators turn increasingly to network sharing (GSM and 3G), helped by regulatory relaxation, and some outsource network infrastructure.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D30 state of affairs in 2003: network-sharing deals and regulatory approvals in major European markets during 2003.
verdicts.reason: The European Commission approved T-Mobile/O2 3G network sharing in the UK in April 2003 and in Germany in July 2003 (site sharing and national roaming), after which T-Mobile and O2 implemented sharing; Sweden's Electronic Communications Act of 24 July 2003 allowed ordering shared use of infrastructure, and Swedish 3G licences allowed sharing up to 70% of radio infrastructure. Both the sharing trend and the regulatory relaxation the report names occurred in 2003. The outsourcing sub-point is not checked.

evidence.shows: EU Commission approved 3G network sharing in the UK in April 2003 (T-Mobile and O2 then entered sharing) and in Germany in July 2003 (site sharing, national roaming exempted); Sweden: licences allow sharing up to 70% of radio infrastructure; Act on Electronic Communications of 24 July 2003 allows mandated shared use.

verdicts.reading: In 2003 European mobile voice revenues stay roughly stable (prices little changed, interconnect cuts phasing in slowly), so data, led by business SMS, MMS, premium SMS and file transfer, is the main driver of revenue growth.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D30 state of affairs in 2003, tested on Vodafone (largest European operator) service revenue split for the year to March 2004.
verdicts.reason: Data grew much faster than voice and gained share (Vodafone data +25% to 16.1% of service revenue from 14.6%; UK data 16.1%), with SMS the largest part of the data growth. But voice did not stay stable: voice revenue rose 11% (GBP +2.4bn) against data's GBP +0.9bn, so voice still supplied about three quarters of service-revenue growth, and voice minutes rose 11% despite termination-rate cuts. Data was the fastest-growing line, not the main driver of growth; MMS did not contribute materially. Part held, part failed, so partial.
